items.content:
Share Hormuz attacks intensify as efforts to end war on Iran stall on social media
US bombs cargo vessel in Gulf of Oman 'trying to run Iran blockade'
Tehran, Iran – Strikes around the strategic Strait of Hormuz have picked up again as mediated efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran remain deadlocked.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said on Saturday night that an unnamed crude oil supertanker hit a naval mine and suffered a major fire while using an unauthorised route in the waterway with navigation systems turned off. In a statement, it warned of a similar fate for any oil tanker that “wishes to ignore the security and rules” of the strait, through which one-fifth of the world’s oil and gas passes in peacetime.
list of 3 items list 1 of 3 Is Trump signalling a return to war with Iran after the midterms?
list 2 of 3 ‘Anachronism’: Rubio’s civilisational rhetoric prompts pushback from Iran
list 3 of 3 US forces disable ship ‘attempting to run’ Iran blockade in Gulf of Oman
On Sunday, a senior Iranian army official told state television that the country’s forces remain prepared for both defensive and offensive operations, more than seven months since the United States and Israel started the war by attacking Iran on February 28.
“We have struck blows against enemy vessels. If anything else happens against Iran, we will strike them again,” said Habibollah Sayyari, chief of staff and joint coordinator of the army.
His comments came after the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported several incidents of military action or warnings against vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman over the past day. It said ship masters in the vicinity of Ras al-Khaimah, in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), had been directed via radio broadcast overnight to move from their anchorages. And on Sunday afternoon, UKMTO reported ⁠an unidentified projectile had struck a tanker ⁠heading outbound through the Strait of ⁠Hormuz.
Separately, the UAE said its coastguard had rescued 22 crew members after a fire broke out at an unnamed tanker close to its shores, although it did not identify the cause of the blaze.
Early on Sunday, the US Central Command (CENTCOM) released footage of a fighter jet bombing the stern of a Panama-flagged cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman and disabling its propulsion to enforce its naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports .
Since the US reimposed the blockade in mid-July, CENTCOM says its forces have disabled four commercial vessels, turned around 135 ships and destroyed 10 tankers linked with Iran. Washington says Tehran has exported no oil through the blockade line.
This comes as at least a dozen ships were attacked over the week ending on October 5, the highest number since the war began. At least one was hit off the north coast of Qatar , signalling that the danger extends beyond the immediate Hormuz passage as Iran and the US vie for control.
The ship attacks appear to have decreased energy flows that had surpassed pre-war levels at the start of the month. Kpler data cited by CNBC on Friday showed that average crude passing through the strait for the week ended October 7 was 8.5 million barrels per day, roughly 40 percent below the normal level.
To reopen the strait and reach a resolution to the war, Iran has demanded a return to a now-collapsed memorandum of understanding that was agreed in June, as well as Washington’s backing of an already finalised Iran-Oman deal that designates temporary coordinated entry and exit routes for vessels transiting the strait.
The Thailand-flagged bulk carrier Mayuree Naree, which was struck by a missile near the Strait of Hormuz, is seen stranded off the coast of Iran’s Qeshm Island [File: Fatemeh Bahrami/Anadolu via Getty Images]
Messages continue to be exchanged between the two sides through mediators, although no breakthrough is expected in the coming weeks leading to the US midterm vote, set to take place on November 3, and Israel’s election, due on October 27.
US Vice President JD Vance said last week that Iran must make a “meaningful” reduction in its nuclear enrichment capacity to end the war, signalling a potential easing of the oft-repeated US demand that zero enrichment must take place on Iranian soil.
Tehran has said a nuclear agreement potentially involving diluting its high-enriched uranium can be part of the later stages of talks, but has emphasised it will not abandon enrichment altogether.
“The achievements of our indigenous nuclear industry cannot be stopped,” Iran’s nuclear chief Mohammad Eslami said during a speech on Sunday, pointing to electricity generation as a main use case.
He also renewed criticism against the International Atomic Energy Agency for not condemning repeated US threats to again bomb Iran’s nuclear facilities .
Behrouz Kamalvandi, spokesman of the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran, told reporters on Sunday that authorities plan on using military and diplomatic avenues to get what they want.
“The Islamic Republic will decisively pursue the country’s interests,” he said. “If those interests can be secured through diplomacy, that is much better, but if not, we will secure them in the field of battle”.

items.content:
Aftermath of a Russian air strike in Kharkiv on Sunday. Photograph: Volodymyr Pavlov/Reuters
Aftermath of a Russian air strike in Kharkiv on Sunday. Photograph: Volodymyr Pavlov/Reuters
Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war as Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’
Ukrainian president earlier rejected US call for Kyiv to stop bombing oil refineries, saying Moscow must first end attacks on energy infrastructure
Donald Trump has announced an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, apparently without consulting Volodymyr Zelenskyy , who said the deal to stop long-range attacks was “news to me”.
In a social media post, the US president claimed the two sides had reached an agreement. “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine . Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on Truth Social.
He offered no further details. Zelenskyy said he was surprised by the announcement but would agree to it if Vladimir Putin did the same. “If President Trump negotiated it with Putin – please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready and we will accept it,” the Ukrainian president told the Axios website.
Earlier, Zelenskyy rebuffed Trump’s demand made on Saturday that Kyiv stop bombing Russian oil refineries. Zelenskyy said Moscow had to first halt its own “brutal” attacks on his country’s energy infrastructure.
Any deal to end long-range drone strikes by Ukraine on targets inside Russia would have to be “reciprocal”, he said. It should be backed by “real guarantees” – meaning punitive measures against Moscow from Ukraine’s allies, including the US.
The aftermath on Sunday of a Russian strike on Kharkiv that hit residential homes. Photograph: Vyacheslav Madiyevskyy/Reuters There was no sign that the Kremlin was observing Trump’s ceasefire. According to Zelenskyy, Russian drones took to the sky “throughout the day” on Sunday. There were also “unfortunately” several airstrikes, he said, including on energy infrastructure.
The Ukrainian president said the Russians hit thermal power station No 5 in the eastern city of Kharkiv – the latest of more than 200 strikes this week against electricity generation and transmission facilities in Ukraine. There were another 17 hits on gas and oil facilities, he added.
The fast-moving row between Washington and Kyiv began on Friday when Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports . He said the move would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections.
A furious Zelenskyy called the decision “weak” and said it would generate “billions” in extra revenue for Putin, enabling him to wage war “even more intensely”. An equally irate Trump said Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraine needed a “new leader” , he said on Saturday.
Map of Ukraine with Russian advances and territory Responding to Trump, Zelenskyy said it was up to Ukrainians to choose “one or another leader”. He told ABC News he was willing to accept Trump’s demands and to organise elections, but only if Putin agreed to a “total” 60-day ceasefire.
The bitter public feud is the most serious between the US and Ukraine since last year, when Trump berated Zelenskyy in the Oval Office .
The Financial Times, citing officials in Europe , reported on Sunday that the US is ⁠threatening ⁠to stop ​the procurement ⁠system that provides ⁠Ukraine ​with ‌weapons to ‌press Kyiv to halt its ‌deep strikes on ​Russian energy infrastructure.
The New York Times has reported that US officials have offered the Kremlin lucrative economic incentives in exchange for a ceasefire. They reportedly include releasing billions in Russian sovereign assets that are frozen. The Trump administration also revisited a plan to sell parts of Russia’s energy company, Lukoil. The multibillion deal would benefit Middle Eastern investors, the paper reported , some with “business ties” to US negotiators.
Medics help a woman injured in a Russian attack on a residential area in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine on Saturday after overnight strikes. Photograph: Daryna Naumova/EPA On Saturday, Trump criticised Zelenskyy and said he had refused to make a deal to end the fighting. In response, Ukraine’s president laid the blame for Europe’s biggest war since 1945 on “Russia and Russia alone”. “It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so,” he said.
Ukrainian officials point out that the White House is demanding Kyiv give up its most effective weapon, without demanding any corresponding concessions from Russia. In recent weeks, Kyiv has dealt a major blow to Russia’s economy, striking oil complexes, warehouses and datacentres.
Russia’s own bombing campaign has been relentless. On Saturday it killed 23 people in the city of Zaporizhzhia, including four children, and hit a five-storey apartment block in the frontline town of Sloviansk. Zelenskyy said Moscow’s aerial campaign involved thousands of aerial bombs and jet-powered drones. It continued “unabated”, he said.
‘A life-or-death race’: the volunteers protecting Kyiv’s skies from new jet-powered drones
The head of Ukraine’s foreign affairs committee, Oleksandr Merezhko , said Trump’s “bullying” demand for Zelenskyy to quit had strengthened him at home “paradoxically”, after recent damaging corruption scandals. “Putin’s plan is to decapitate Zelenskyy and remove him as a wartime leader. Trump is siding with Putin,” Merezhko said.
He added: “I’m afraid that behind this situation is Trump’s worldview. He wants to do business with Putin. For him, Ukraine seems like an obstacle to be removed. Both Trump and Putin wish to pressure us into capitulation.”
Referring to the notorious 1939 agreement between Nazi Germany and the USSR, Merezhko said: “We are moving to a new Molotov-Ribbentrop pact and to a world of strongmen and spheres of influence.”
Merezhko said Ukraine would continue to destroy enemy oil refineries, against US wishes, because they funded Russia’s war machine and acknowledged that a cutoff of US intelligence sharing with Kyiv – threatened by the Trump administration – would “blind” Ukraine’s air defence systems. “This would be an act of complicity with Putin’s genocide. It would mean more dead civilians and dead children,” he said.
Ukrainian negotiators had been meeting in Florida with their American counterparts, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, when Trump announced the US was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel. Blindsided, the Ukrainians went home early. “It felt like a trap,” one stunned Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent newspaper .
On Sunday, Zelenskyy shored up support in a series of conversations with key allies including Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, the Polish leader, Donald Tusk, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen.
Earlier Zelenskyy spoke with the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, and the Finnish president, Alexander Stubb. Downing Street said Burnham recognised the last 24 hours had been “difficult” for Ukraine and “reiterated his complete solidarity”.
Downing Street said the two leaders agreed “to maintain pressure on Russia” and to strengthen the sanctions regime, despite Trump’s efforts to the contrary. “Russia should agree to an immediate energy ceasefire, ending its brutal strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure and its attacks on shipping in the Black Sea,” a statement added.
Speaking over the weekend, Zelenskyy said Trump’s decision empowered Putin and gave him “extra money for the war”, running into millions and “perhaps billions”. “It is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should act. And, in my view, it is a weak decision,” he said.

items.content:
Donald Trump has twice rejected Saudi appeals for help. Photograph: Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images
Donald Trump has twice rejected Saudi appeals for help. Photograph: Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images
Houthi attack on Riyadh airport forces swift rethink of Trump’s new strategy
US president’s plan to park the wars in Iran and Yemen, while blaming Ukraine for diesel prices, looks unsustainable
The reckless missile attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh on Saturday did not just export the death and misery inside Yemen to Saudi Arabia, it also left Donald Trump forced to reconsider his diplomatic and political strategy designed to take him into the midterm elections next month.
The US president’s plan had only been unveiled on Friday. He said it was the result of “a world problem” – spiralling diesel prices – which he blamed on Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s attacks on Russian oil refineries. He was going to keep the political temperature down on his war of choice in Iran and its spillover in Yemen until after the midterms.
In pursuit of this strategy, he claimed the Iranian blockade in the strait of Hormuz was in effect broken, producing figures on daily oil barrel exports to assuage the markets. As a further insurance he also claimed it was impossible to negotiate with the Iranians since there was no single leadership in Tehran.
Saudi Arabia, in conjunction with Turkey, and Pakistan, were largely to be left to sort out the Houthis along the Red Sea. The fate of Yemen, the poorest country in the world according to the International Monetary Fund, was not going to shift votes in Kansas or Alaska.
Now, after the Riyadh airport attack, it is doubtful, for a basket of reasons, that this anyway threadbare strategy, largely born of desperation, can hold.
For all the talk of the Gulf becoming responsible for its own security, it is doubtful that Saudi Arabia can be left to fend for itself after the carnage in Riyadh. One of the the 12 dead is an American and there may be more among the severely injured. Something is clearly wrong with Saudi defences since the Houthis are firing rockets from 500 miles away, and they are reaching their target too often.
The US has had a unilateral ceasefire with the Houthis since 2025, and once the hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis recommenced in the summer, the pact was quietly renewed. Trump has twice rejected Saudi appeals for help. Can he spurn them three times? The pressure to act as allies are expected to may prove overwhelming.
But “the blame Zelenskyy, trade with Russia” strategy is anyway unlikely to work. The amount of additional diesel Vladimir Putin will put on the market is not enough to bring down prices at the pump. Russia accounted for about 12% of global diesel shipped by sea. Exports have fallen by about a third, according to calculations by the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air.
The deal has also reawakened Europe’s worst fears about Trump’s relationship with Russia only weeks after Congress had passed a sanctions package against Moscow authorising Trump to penalise buyers of Russian energy.
Europeans know full well that the inflation problem helping to drive populism is caused by the Iran war and not by Zelenskyy’s tactics. The only question is who will say so. The former UK Conservative prime minister Boris Johnson did not hold back, writing: “It is sickening that the USA is now lifting sanctions on Russian fuel, and transparently ridiculous to blame Ukraine for the spike in prices that obviously began with the closure of the strait of Hormuz. Putin is murdering innocent Ukrainian civilians every day. The Ukrainians are fighting for their lives. And yet the White House is apparently determined to force American drivers to bankroll Putin’s slaughter.”
The German education minister and a member of the CDU, Karin Prien, said: “For a few litres of diesel. What moral bankruptcy.”
Mark Rutte, the Nato secretary general and Trump ally, will this week travel to Estonia, one of the countries most supportive of Ukraine. He will have some explaining to do. Estonia’s foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, vowed that EU foreign ministers on Monday will impose the biggest package of sanctions in its history, and he, along with Sweden, now wants to revisit using frozen Russian assets to help Ukraine.
What is worse, it looks as if the political damage to the Republicans caused by the Iran war is irrecoverable. Polls show the ship has sailed. The war has already been weaponised as a pocketbook issue by every Democratic candidate in every TV debate. Republican candidates, challenged to disown the war, are scrambling for the relative safety of identity politics.
The Iranians are also trying to maximise the damage they cause in the strait of Hormuz, countering the Trump narrative that the blockade has been broken. Scenes of tankers on fire are proliferating.
So Trump post-Riyadh needs to rethink. He can rejoin the war against the Houthis, ending the unilateral US ceasefire, but, if so, he knows from experience this will be costly. The first three weeks of the war against Iran cost $1bn a day. Many of the US president’s advisers say he may as well also attack Iran, the Houthis’ backers, as Tehran expects him to do. The Iranian military nevertheless still believes it has escalation dominance, and what happened in Riyadh can be repeated across the Gulf.
The alternative is that his team can negotiate discreetly and indirectly with Tehran as is occurring in Doha. Some Iranians are urging their leadership to seize the chance, arguing Trump is uniquely vulnerable in the run-up to the midterms.
A deal could be done, including on uranium enrichment, but it would not be palatable for the US – or for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu’s re-election chances.
China and Russia are trying to sort out the Houthis diplomatically, but the Houthi objectives are broadening, while the south of Yemen is split about its future inside the country, a division that harms the country’s ability to be the ground component that Saudi Arabia needs to supplement its air-power dominance. Taiz, the third city of Yemen, is struggling to overcome a Houthi siege. The Saudis can deliver retribution, but retribution is not a solution to a decade-long civil war.
So for the moment the twin Trump strategy – to park the Iran and Yemen conflicts while blaming Zelenskyy – is now so transparent, so morally craven, and in its own terms so ineffective, that it looks unsustainable. The only question is whether the strategy will be jettisoned by the president or instead just rejected by the American people at the ballot box.

JOEL ROSE, HOST: President Trump blames the Russia-Ukraine war for soaring energy costs. The war with Iran, though, is the dominant factor keeping global diesel prices high. This weekend, the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations Centre reported two oil tankers traversing the Strait of Hormuz were attacked. Nearly a hundred vessels have been hit since the U.S. war with Iran began, resulting in two dozen deaths, according to the U.N. And the attacks are taking on new forms. MANOJ YADAV: Small boats that surrounded a few of the vessels and started firing with RPG and even with the guns. ROSE: Manoj Yadav is the general secretary of a union representing merchant sailors from India - many of whom work in the Persian Gulf. He says because of that danger, ship captains and sailors making these transits are being offered big money. YADAV: Not only one time, two time, three times - five times of their salary they are getting just to transit the Hormuz Strait. ROSE: Five times their regular salary. YADAV: Yeah. ROSE: And if they don't comply, Yadav says they might be punished. YADAV: And maybe there are possibility that they will get blacklisted. ROSE: Now, oil deliveries through the Strait of Hormuz have recently seen a recovery, maybe as much as 80% of the pre-war supply, according to trade intelligence firm Kpler. But the cost of getting through the choke point continues to hit pocketbooks around the world. And in the U.S., that's raising the political stakes ahead of the midterm elections.

items.content:
Saudi Arabia, UAE Increase Oil Exports as Hormuz Shipments Recover | Egypt Oil & Gas
Saudi Arabia, UAE Increase Oil Exports as Hormuz Shipments Recover
Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) have increased crude oil exports as shipments through the Strait of Hormuz recover, with both countries seeking to regain market share lost during the Iran war, according to data from analytics firm Kpler cited by Reuters on October 8.
Crude oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz averaged 12 million barrels per day (bbl/d) over the two weeks preceding the report, around 80% of pre-war levels, Kpler's data showed.
Middle Eastern crude oil exports exceeded the pre-war average of 18 million bbl/d for much of the week ending October 3, including shipments through alternative routes.
The UAE alone has exported an average of 3.3 million bbl/d of crude oil since June, broadly matching pre-war levels, while its total production averaged approximately 4.2 million bbl/d over the same period, above its pre-war average of 3.9 million bbl/d, according to Kpler.
Saudi Arabia initially redirected large volumes of crude oil to Yanbu on the Red Sea after the war began, keeping exports near 60% of pre-war levels during much of the conflict.
However, attacks on the East-West pipeline in September and Houthi attacks affecting the Bab el-Mandeb Strait disrupted the strategy, prompting the kingdom to redirect more shipments through Hormuz.
Saudi crude oil exports subsequently averaged approximately 7.3 million bbl/d over the three weeks preceding the report, approaching pre-war levels, according to Kpler.
However, Saudi production is expected to average 7.4 million bbl/d in October, around 75% of pre-war levels, reflecting reduced domestic refining capacity following strikes on processing facilities.
Saudi Arabia's share of Asian crude oil imports fell from 24% in February to a record low of 9% in September, but is expected to recover to approximately 14% in October, while the UAE's share declined from 13% in February to 12% in October, based on Reuters calculations using Kpler data.

items.content:
US President Donald Trump and Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky at the United Nations General Assembly on September 22, 2026, in New York City. Press Service Of The President Of Ukraine/AP
Get your news from a source that’s not owned and controlled by oligarchs. Sign up for the free Mother Jones Daily .
President Donald Trump keeps pointing the finger at everyone for surging fuel prices but himself. Over the weekend, he once again blamed Ukraine, asserting that the country's retaliatory airstrikes on Russia's oil refineries were causing prices to spike. Now Trump is urging Ukraine to scrap its leader.
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does,” Trump said on Saturday, suggesting that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has not done enough to broker a peace deal with Russia.
For weeks, Trump has called on Zelenskyy to stop striking Russia's energy infrastructure, claiming that the attacks are “ hurting the world ,” while saying virtually nothing about Russia's strikes against Ukraine.
Responding to Trump's escalatory remarks, Zelenskyy on Sunday criticized Trump's framing, telling ABC News that it is near universally understood that the closing of the Strait of Hormuz has led to higher prices—not Ukraine's strikes against Russia. But according to Zelenskyy, it’s easier for Trump to blame Ukraine instead of acknowledging the United States' overwhelming role in surging prices around the world.
“People have to hear reality,” the Ukrainian president said. “Don’t play games with people.”
Zelenskyy: "Prices are rising because of the war in the Middle East, the blocking of Hormuz. Everyone understands it. If we want to speak with people fairly, if we want to be clear, if we want to speak with our nations openly, people have to hear reality. Don't play games with people."
— Aaron Rupar (@atrupar.com) 2026-10-11T13:49:23.365Z
Later on Sunday, Trump claimed on Truth Social that there is now an "ENERGY CEASEFIRE" in the war between Russia and Ukraine. But he gave little detail about what that entailed.
The head-spinning war of words follows Trump's deal on Friday to allow Russia to supply diesel to other countries, an apparent bid to bring down prices ahead of the midterm elections. But just last month , Trump had signed a bill granting him power to impose up to 100 percent tariffs on top countries that buy Russian oil or gas, namely China and India .
Even GOP lawmakers have voiced rare opposition to the deal. Rep. Michael McCaul (R-Texas) wrote on X that he was “concerned the lifting of sanctions on Russian oil will only fund the Kremlin’s war machine—emboldening more violence and destruction, as we have seen in recent days.”
Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) said that Trump should use his new sanctioning authority against Russia instead of allowing the country to “rake in revenues, and continue its catastrophic war in Ukraine.”
On Saturday, Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) announced plans for a bipartisan bill that he said would prevent the president from lifting sanctions. “[Ukrainian] President Volodymyr Zelensky has the overwhelming support of the United States Congress, he has the overwhelming support of the American people, and he has the overwhelming support of the Ukrainian people,” Fitzpatrick wrote on social media .

items.title: Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war as Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’ - The Guardian
items.summary: Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war as Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’  The Guardian
items.content:
Aftermath of a Russian air strike in Kharkiv on Sunday. Photograph: Volodymyr Pavlov/Reuters
Aftermath of a Russian air strike in Kharkiv on Sunday. Photograph: Volodymyr Pavlov/Reuters
Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war as Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’
Ukrainian president earlier rejected US call for Kyiv to stop bombing oil refineries, saying Moscow must first end attacks on energy infrastructure
Donald Trump has announced an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, apparently without consulting Volodymyr Zelenskyy , who said the deal to stop long-range attacks was “news to me”.
In a social media post, the US president claimed the two sides had reached an agreement. “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine . Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on Truth Social.
He offered no further details. Zelenskyy said he was surprised by the announcement but would agree to it if Vladimir Putin did the same. “If President Trump negotiated it with Putin – please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready and we will accept it,” the Ukrainian president told the Axios website.
Earlier, Zelenskyy rebuffed Trump’s demand made on Saturday that Kyiv stop bombing Russian oil refineries. Zelenskyy said Moscow had to first halt its own “brutal” attacks on his country’s energy infrastructure.
Any deal to end long-range drone strikes by Ukraine on targets inside Russia would have to be “reciprocal”, he said. It should be backed by “real guarantees” – meaning punitive measures against Moscow from Ukraine’s allies, including the US.
The aftermath on Sunday of a Russian strike on Kharkiv that hit residential homes. Photograph: Vyacheslav Madiyevskyy/Reuters There was no sign that the Kremlin was observing Trump’s ceasefire. According to Zelenskyy, Russian drones took to the sky “throughout the day” on Sunday. There were also “unfortunately” several airstrikes, he said, including on energy infrastructure.
The Ukrainian president said the Russians hit thermal power station No 5 in the eastern city of Kharkiv – the latest of more than 200 strikes this week against electricity generation and transmission facilities in Ukraine. There were another 17 hits on gas and oil facilities, he added.
The fast-moving row between Washington and Kyiv began on Friday when Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports . He said the move would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections.
A furious Zelenskyy called the decision “weak” and said it would generate “billions” in extra revenue for Putin, enabling him to wage war “even more intensely”. An equally irate Trump said Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraine needed a “new leader” , he said on Saturday.
Map of Ukraine with Russian advances and territory Responding to Trump, Zelenskyy said it was up to Ukrainians to choose “one or another leader”. He told ABC News he was willing to accept Trump’s demands and to organise elections, but only if Putin agreed to a “total” 60-day ceasefire.
The bitter public feud is the most serious between the US and Ukraine since last year, when Trump berated Zelenskyy in the Oval Office .
The Financial Times, citing officials in Europe , reported on Sunday that the US is ⁠threatening ⁠to stop ​the procurement ⁠system that provides ⁠Ukraine ​with ‌weapons to ‌press Kyiv to halt its ‌deep strikes on ​Russian energy infrastructure.
The New York Times has reported that US officials have offered the Kremlin lucrative economic incentives in exchange for a ceasefire. They reportedly include releasing billions in Russian sovereign assets that are frozen. The Trump administration also revisited a plan to sell parts of Russia’s energy company, Lukoil. The multibillion deal would benefit Middle Eastern investors, the paper reported , some with “business ties” to US negotiators.
Medics help a woman injured in a Russian attack on a residential area in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine on Saturday after overnight strikes. Photograph: Daryna Naumova/EPA On Saturday, Trump criticised Zelenskyy and said he had refused to make a deal to end the fighting. In response, Ukraine’s president laid the blame for Europe’s biggest war since 1945 on “Russia and Russia alone”. “It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so,” he said.
Ukrainian officials point out that the White House is demanding Kyiv give up its most effective weapon, without demanding any corresponding concessions from Russia. In recent weeks, Kyiv has dealt a major blow to Russia’s economy, striking oil complexes, warehouses and datacentres.
Russia’s own bombing campaign has been relentless. On Saturday it killed 23 people in the city of Zaporizhzhia, including four children, and hit a five-storey apartment block in the frontline town of Sloviansk. Zelenskyy said Moscow’s aerial campaign involved thousands of aerial bombs and jet-powered drones. It continued “unabated”, he said.
‘A life-or-death race’: the volunteers protecting Kyiv’s skies from new jet-powered drones
The head of Ukraine’s foreign affairs committee, Oleksandr Merezhko , said Trump’s “bullying” demand for Zelenskyy to quit had strengthened him at home “paradoxically”, after recent damaging corruption scandals. “Putin’s plan is to decapitate Zelenskyy and remove him as a wartime leader. Trump is siding with Putin,” Merezhko said.
He added: “I’m afraid that behind this situation is Trump’s worldview. He wants to do business with Putin. For him, Ukraine seems like an obstacle to be removed. Both Trump and Putin wish to pressure us into capitulation.”
Referring to the notorious 1939 agreement between Nazi Germany and the USSR, Merezhko said: “We are moving to a new Molotov-Ribbentrop pact and to a world of strongmen and spheres of influence.”
Merezhko said Ukraine would continue to destroy enemy oil refineries, against US wishes, because they funded Russia’s war machine and acknowledged that a cutoff of US intelligence sharing with Kyiv – threatened by the Trump administration – would “blind” Ukraine’s air defence systems. “This would be an act of complicity with Putin’s genocide. It would mean more dead civilians and dead children,” he said.
Ukrainian negotiators had been meeting in Florida with their American counterparts, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, when Trump announced the US was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel. Blindsided, the Ukrainians went home early. “It felt like a trap,” one stunned Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent newspaper .
On Sunday, Zelenskyy shored up support in a series of conversations with key allies including Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, the Polish leader, Donald Tusk, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen.
Earlier Zelenskyy spoke with the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, and the Finnish president, Alexander Stubb. Downing Street said Burnham recognised the last 24 hours had been “difficult” for Ukraine and “reiterated his complete solidarity”.
Downing Street said the two leaders agreed “to maintain pressure on Russia” and to strengthen the sanctions regime, despite Trump’s efforts to the contrary. “Russia should agree to an immediate energy ceasefire, ending its brutal strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure and its attacks on shipping in the Black Sea,” a statement added.
Speaking over the weekend, Zelenskyy said Trump’s decision empowered Putin and gave him “extra money for the war”, running into millions and “perhaps billions”. “It is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should act. And, in my view, it is a weak decision,” he said.
Luke Harding’s Betrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest is published by Guardian Faber

items.title: Warren Buffett warns of stock market risks as S&P 500 valuation tops 40 - Beinsure
items.summary: Warren Buffett warns of stock market risks as S&P 500 valuation tops 40  Beinsure
items.content:
Warren Buffett warns of stock market risks as S&P 500 valuation tops 40
How investors can manage stock market correction risks
U.S. stocks have continued their strong rally, with the S&P 500 gaining approximately 19% over the past six months and the Nasdaq advancing 26%. Both indexes reached record highs this week, extending a period of market gains that has raised concerns about valuations and speculative investment behavior.
Warren Buffett has repeatedly warned during 2026 about the risks of investors buying stocks primarily because prices are rising rather than because underlying businesses justify their valuations.
The S&P 500 has gained approximately 19% over six months, while the Nasdaq has risen 26%, with both indexes reaching record highs amid concerns about speculative trading.
The S&P 500 Shiller CAPE ratio has remained above 40 since May 2026, compared with a historical average of approximately 17 and a record of 44 before the dot-com crash.
Warren Buffett's caution and Berkshire Hathaway's preference for holding cash have renewed attention to earnings quality, debt levels, portfolio concentration and valuation risks.
The concern is particularly relevant as share prices advance faster than corporate earnings. Berkshire Hathaway's decision to maintain substantial cash holdings rather than deploy more capital has also attracted attention, although its cash position alone does not establish a forecast for market performance.
One valuation measure suggests that investors are paying historically elevated prices for U.S. equities.
The S&P 500 Shiller cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio, commonly known as CAPE, has remained above 40 since May 2026.
The measure compares stock prices with average inflation-adjusted earnings over the preceding 10 years, providing a longer-term assessment of valuations than conventional earnings multiples.
Its historical average is approximately 17. The ratio reached a record of 44 in late 1999, shortly before the technology-driven market bubble burst in March 2000.
A CAPE reading above 40 does not predict an imminent correction. It does indicate that investors are paying substantially more for earnings than historical norms, potentially increasing the market's sensitivity to disappointing financial results or changes in sentiment.
The technology boom of the late 1990s provides a useful reference for understanding the risks associated with elevated valuations.
Hundreds of technology companies experienced substantial share price increases as investors placed aggressive expectations on their future growth.
When the bubble collapsed in early 2000, many businesses suffered severe losses, particularly those with weak balance sheets, unsustainable business models and limited profitability.
Companies with established earnings, manageable debt and durable competitive advantages were generally better positioned to withstand the downturn.
The distinction between share price performance and underlying business quality became particularly important once investor enthusiasm weakened.
Today's leading technology companies may have stronger financial fundamentals than many businesses that attracted speculative investment during the dot-com era. Nevertheless, rising valuations can create risks even when the underlying companies are profitable.
Buffett's concern centers on investor behavior that treats recent price appreciation as sufficient justification for purchasing shares, without assessing whether expected future earnings support those prices.
According to Fortune, Buffett has warned that a speculative or gambling-oriented investment culture can push valuations higher across the market, including for businesses whose financial performance does not justify the increase.
Elevated market valuations do not necessarily require investors to liquidate their equity holdings. They do, however, provide a reason to reassess company fundamentals and portfolio risks.
Profitability is an important starting point. Businesses generating consistent earnings and operating cash flow have financial resources that can support operations during periods of weaker investor sentiment.
Companies dependent primarily on expectations of future revenue growth may be more vulnerable when market conditions deteriorate.
Debt levels also matter. Heavily leveraged businesses can face greater financial pressure when borrowing costs rise, credit availability tightens or revenue growth slows. Stronger balance sheets provide more flexibility during economic downturns.
Valuation deserves similar scrutiny. Stocks trading at high earnings multiples require substantial future growth to justify their current prices. If those expectations depend heavily on developments that have not yet materialized, investors face the possibility of significant repricing.
Portfolio concentration presents another risk. A small number of strongly performing stocks may account for a disproportionate share of portfolio gains and total exposure following a sustained rally.
Such concentration can increase vulnerability if the companies responsible for earlier gains experience simultaneous declines.
How investors can manage stock market correction risks
Attempting to identify the exact market peak is difficult, and poorly timed trading decisions can undermine long-term investment returns.
A more practical approach is to review portfolio allocations before a potential downturn rather than waiting until losses force difficult decisions.
Following six months of substantial market gains, the relative weight of equities or individual holdings may have increased beyond an investor's intended allocation. Rebalancing can bring those exposures back into line with financial objectives and risk tolerance.
Regular investing through dollar-cost averaging offers another way to reduce dependence on market timing. Investing fixed amounts at predetermined intervals generally results in purchasing fewer shares when prices are elevated and more when prices decline.
The approach does not eliminate market risk or guarantee superior returns, but it allows investors to maintain a consistent investment schedule without needing to predict short-term price movements.
Investment horizons remain an important consideration. Funds needed within the next two or three years may be unsuitable for substantial equity exposure because a market decline could occur before the money is required.
Buffett's warnings should therefore be understood as a caution about speculative behavior and the relationship between asset prices and underlying financial performance, rather than a prediction of an imminent stock market crash.
With the S&P 500 CAPE ratio above 40 and major indexes trading near record highs, earnings quality, financial resilience, valuation discipline and portfolio diversification remain central considerations for investors assessing their exposure to U.S. equities.

VW is exhibiting at the Paris show for the first time in 20 years, unveiling its new all-electric ID Tiguan. Photograph: Volkswagen AG
VW is exhibiting at the Paris show for the first time in 20 years, unveiling its new all-electric ID Tiguan. Photograph: Volkswagen AG
Volkswagen boss backs EU plan to bolster domestic European industry
Oliver Blume says ‘Made in Europe’ rules to counter rapid rise of lower-price Chinese brands ‘must reward real value creation’
The boss of Volkswagen has backed EU proposals to boost its domestic industry, arguing European carmakers need to be able to “compete under comparable conditions” with Chinese rivals.
Oliver Blume said “Made in Europe” rules from the EU “must reward real value creation in Europe”, speaking in Paris before the motor show this week.
The rules are aimed at countering the rapid rise of Chinese brands in Europe in the automotive sector and other important manufacturing industries. Lower-priced Chinese manufacturers have prompted a crisis in several industries.
Volkswagen is among the most-affected European companies. Germany’s biggest carmaker has launched a brutal plan to cut as many as 100,000 jobs . Blume said it was the “largest transformation programme in its history”.
Alarm bells sound in Brussels as EU sales of Chinese hybrid cars rocket
The proposals for the Made in Europe rules, formally known as the Industrial Accelerator Act, would limit subsidies and public procurement to products with a large proportion of their materials and manufacturing coming from within the EU.
Blume listed a litany of challenges facing European carmakers, saying: “Europe is under enormous competitive pressure.” These included: high energy costs; lower demand as consumers struggle with high inflation; the need to be quicker to develop cars; and intense competition from China .
On Friday, the EU said it had reached a landmark deal with China to “halve” its sales of hybrid cars in the bloc amid fears surging sales could kill off parts of the European car industry.
Blume said Germany’s carmakers were happy to compete with Chinese rivals, but said the EU should try to reward businesses with significant European footprints.
“Companies that invest and develop in Europe must see a clear benefit,” he said.
Referring to Chinese companies, he added: “Those who sell here should compete under comparable conditions and create jobs and value here in Europe, too.
The new all-electric ID Tiguan. Photograph: Volkswagen AG Blume added: “We believe in open markets, but openness also means standing up for our own interests in Europe. Because a strong industrial base means more than economic success. It protects technological independence.”
Volkswagen is exhibiting at the Paris show for the first time in 20 years. Blume emphasised the “close ties between France and Germany”, while hosting the French industry minister, Sébastian Martin.
Arno Antlitz, VW’s chief financial officer, said the job cuts were necessary to “increase our economic power” by increasing profitability and allowing it to defend its “home turf”.
The company is cutting the number of models it offers worldwide from 150 to 75 across brands including Audi and Škoda. It hopes the move will reduce complexity in its factories and for dealers, cutting the cost of each vehicle it makes.
On Sunday, it revealed the production version of its ID Tiguan, an electric edition of its bestselling family SUV.

items.content:
Diesel prices have risen dramatically since the US war on Iran. Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/AFP/Getty Images
Diesel prices have risen dramatically since the US war on Iran. Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/AFP/Getty Images
Trump’s deal with Putin will have little impact on US diesel prices, experts say
Analysts say fuel will take weeks to ship and quantity is too small to affect prices, while full deal is unlikely to be met given damage to Russian refineries
Trump announces partial ceasefire but Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’
Donald Trump’s deal with Vladimir Putin to temporarily lift sanctions on US imports of Russian diesel will have little “meaningful” effect on motorists and businesses in the US and overseas, energy and foreign policy analysts have predicted.
The US president infuriated Volodymyr Zelenskyy when he announced the deal on Friday, writing on Truth Social that the agreement with his Russia counterpart to supply millions of tonnes of diesel was essential to reduce fuel prices in the US, which have soared after his decision to go to war against Iran.
The package announced by Trump involves 300,000 tonnes of diesel released immediately “to the American and global marketplace” followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and a further 1m tonnes after that. The 300,000 figure equates to about three-quarters of what the US would use in a day, according to calculations using figures from the US Energy Information Administration .
“Diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my greatest priority,” Trump posted.
However, experts suggested that the quantities involved – and the time it will take for the supplies to arrive in the US – is “too little, too late” to affect current high diesel prices, which observers have linked to challenging Republican party polling numbers before next month’s midterm elections.
Graph showing increase in price of US diesel US prices have surged by almost 70% since the start of the Iran war, to about $6.30 a gallon , according to American Automobile Association. In the UK, the average price of diesel climbed to a record £2 a litre earlier in October, and sat just below that mark on Friday.
Ashley Kelty, an energy analyst with the investment bank Panmure Liberum, said: “It is not going to have any impact on prices. The first amount [due to be shipped to the US] is so small.
“They are going to have to charter vessels, load them and transport the cargo to the US. That will take about three weeks – so we are pretty much at the end of the month and about a week before the midterms.”
The US Treasury secretary, Scott ⁠Bessent, said on Sunday: “This is ​good ‌for the ​American ​people … bringing these diesel prices down.”
However, Kelty said the diesel shipments would also cause complications in a global supply chain, including multinational companies having to work out which of its supplies originated from Russia and therefore might breach sanctions in other jurisdictions, including Europe .
The US Treasury suspended sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, while keeping in place other sanctions on Russian products.
Zelenskyy described Trump’s deal as a “weak decision”, saying it would encourage Russia to keep attacking Ukraine, but Trump then blamed Kyiv’s strikes on Russian energy infrastructure for rising fuel prices. Trump said Ukraine neeeded “a new leader” .
On Sunday, Zelenskyy said he would be ready to stop hitting Russian oil refineries if Russia curbed its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Trump later posted on Truth Social: “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine . Both parties have agreed. Do not break it! Thank you for your attention to this matter.”
Maximilian Hess, the founder of the political risk consultancy Enmetena Advisory and a fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute, said: “It will not have any meaningful domestic US effect or international effect given its full terms are highly unlikely to be met as a result of the impact of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refining which have limited its diesel output.
“The whole point of the deal for Putin is that it fails, which he can blame on Ukraine and thus stoke tensions between Trump and Zelenskyy. Indeed, it’s already working.”

Dow Jones, S&P 500, Nasdaq 100 Outlook: Top Stock Market News This Week
The Dow Jones , S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 have held steady in recent weeks as investors have focused on rising US bond yields and the escalating situation in the Middle East. Their resilience will be tested in the coming weeks as major US companies report earnings and key economic data is released.
Dow Jones, S&P 500, and Nasdaq 100 to React to Earnings Season
The main catalyst for the US stock market this week will be the upcoming earnings season , which will kick off on Tuesday. Top US banks, including popular names like Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan, will release their numbers. Other non-bank companies that will release their numbers are Johnson & Johnson, UnitedHealth Group and Kinder Morgan.
Analysts are optimistic about this earnings season. FactSet (NYSE: FDS ) data shows that the estimate among analysts is that earnings growth will be 29.5%. Historically, the real earnings growth tends to be 7% above the estimate. As such, there is a likelihood that the growth will be over 40%.
The earnings growth comes at a time when American stocks are trading at discount levels. For example, the forward price-to-earnings ratio for the S&P 500 Index is 19.1, lower than the five and ten-year averages.
Why Micron Stock is Struggling Despite Revenue Growth and a Low Valuation
Micron stock price has remained inside a narrow range in the past few days despite its strong revenue growth and cheap valuation
The stock market will also react to the upcoming US consumer price index (CPI) report on Wednesday. Economists expect the data to show that the headline and core CPI numbers rose last month as gasoline and diesel prices jumped.
The average estimate among analysts is that the headline CPI rose from 3.4% in August to 3.6% in September. Core inflation, which excludes the volatile food and energy prices, is expected to come in at 2.5%, up slightly from the previous 2.4%.
These numbers will provide more hints about what to expect from the Federal Reserve. Economists expect the bank to leave rates unchanged in this meeting and then hike in December.
The stock market will also react to the bond market , where the ten-year and five-year yields have pulled back in the past few days.
The US stock market will also react to the ongoing crisis in the Middle East, which is escalating. For example, Yemen’s Houthis launched a major attack against Saudi Arabia’s main airport, with President Donald Trump hinting that the US will intervene .
Iran has also continued striking ships crossing the Strait of Hormuz. There is also fear that the crisis will escalate. If this happens, it means that crude oil prices will continue rising in the coming weeks. This, in turn, will lead to higher inflation, pushing the Fed to hike interest rates, which may affect the stock market.

items.title: Iran war threatens Healey's Budget plans, think tank warns
items.summary: The impact of the Iran war poses significant risks for the government’s spending plans, the Institute for Fiscal Studies says.
items.content:
By Dharshini David ,Â  Deputy economics editor Â  and Â  Tom Espiner ,Â  Business reporter
The price spike caused by the US-Israel war in Iran poses a major challenge for Chancellor John Healey as he puts together his first Budget, an influential think tank has warned.
Higher-than-expected inflation could eat into what the government hoped to spend on public services, meaning Healey will have to choose between spending cuts, tax rises, or a mixture of both, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said.
It urged the government to ensure its spending plans are credible, as opposed to proposing unrealistic future cuts to make the Budget add up.
The Treasury declined to comment on "rumour and speculation".
However, speaking ahead of the annual International Monetary Fund meeting this week, Healey said: "The consequences of conflict in the Middle East and Europe are hitting countries worldwide, leading to higher prices at the pumps and more expensive mortgages at home.
"But Britain and our alliesâ¯can face up to these challenges together."
He said his Budget "will build on this approach with fiscal discipline helping to deliver economic resilience" and give people "breathing space".
However, the government is under growing pressure to show financial markets that it has a tight grip on finances as the cost of borrowing rises.
The IFS cautioned Healey about making any spending announcements in the 28 October Budget speech he has no intention of honouring.
"A 'steady-as-she-goes' Budget is not an option available to the chancellor," said IFS director Helen Miller said.
"Choosing to stay the course with the inherited tax and spending plans would mean allowing inflation to blow departments' spending plans off course.
"Simply pencilling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the Budget a work of fiction," she added.
The US-Israel war against Iran and Russia's invasion of Ukraine have together helped drive up energy prices around the world.
These higher costs have been passed to customers via higher prices on shelves and at the pumps.
The wars have also contributed to a rise in the cost of UK government debt interest payments, adding to the pressure on Healey.
Although higher inflation will boost tax revenues, it will also eat into the value of departments' cash budgets, the IFS said.
Like other analysts, the IFS thinks recent turbulence on bond markets and higher inflation will add around Â£10bn to forecasts for the government's borrowing costs in 2029-30.
However, it still expects the government to meet its self-imposed fiscal rules - that it will only borrow for investment projects by the financial year 2029-30 and also be reducing debt as a percentage of GDP - not least as inflation pushes up tax revenues.
But it expects those rules to be met by a smaller buffer - known as "headroom" - of around Â£20bn. That is less than the Â£24bn buffer predicted at the time of the Spring Statement by the official forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).
Recent indications have been that the markets would be comfortable with that degree of reduced headroom. The IFS also expects any "breathing space" help for households to be temporary and limited in scale.
However, the IFS warns that in such a volatile environment, its forecasts are exceptionally uncertain. And the official forecast from the OBR - which the chancellor relies on when making his plans - may come to a very different conclusion.
The IFS reckons that to maintain departments' budgets in the face of higher inflation, the government may need to find an extra Â£25bn in 2029-30.
That is before consider considering the ambition to raise defence spending. Raising such an amount would point to significant tax rises.
The chancellor does not have to address spending totals in this Budget, and may choose to leave such decisions until future events - for example, next year's Spring Statement or Spending Review - by which time the outlook for the economy could look very different.
But the IFS warned that the spending plans inherited from the previous chancellor, Rachel Reeves, would mean some departments' budgets would not keep pace with inflation in a few years time.
It said not addressing this would cast doubt on the credibility of the government's plans.
However, previous chancellors have relied on a similar strategy of pencilling in unrealistic future spending plans to ensure that they meet the fiscal rules on the day - only to change the plans further down the line.

items.title: South Carolina Senate rivals spar over Iran war, AI and Trump in fiery debate - NBC News
items.summary: South Carolina Senate rivals spar over Iran war, AI and Trump in fiery debate  NBC News
items.content:
Democrat Annie Andrews and Republican Sen. Darline Graham debated exactly three months after Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., died. Getty; Bloomberg via Getty
Republican Sen. Darline Graham of South Carolina and Democratic challenger Annie Andrews clashed Sunday night in their first and perhaps only debate of the general election, tangling over President Donald Trump’s “one big, beautiful bill,” the high costs of gas and goods, the Iran war and AI data centers.
South Carolina is a ruby-red state where Trump remains popular among Republican voters. But the race has tightened in the closing stretch of the campaign, and Democrats believe they have a shot at knocking off Graham, who was appointed to fill her brother Lindsey Graham’s Senate seat after his sudden death in July. The top Senate Republican super PAC has pledged to spend $5 million to shore up Graham’s campaign.
At the start of the debate, hosted in Columbia by South Carolina ETV , Darline Graham noted that Sunday night marked exactly three months since her brother unexpectedly died at age 71.
Andrews, a pediatrician, sought to portray Graham, who previously led a state agency, as an inexperienced empty suit who refuses to stand up to Trump or his unpopular policies. She mocked Graham as “the White House’s ambassador to South Carolina.”
Graham attacked Andrews as the “most radical liberal” to run in South Carolina and as sympathetic to the Democratic Socialist Party. “Annie Andrews will not stand up to the Socialist Democratic Party; she’s only going to join them,” Graham said — a characterization Andrews rejected.
Graham has “been told to come out here and call me Bernie, Ocasio, Mamdani — that’s what’s in her script. But the truth is my name is Annie Andrews, and there shouldn’t be any confusion about that,” Andrews said. “The truth is I support the Second Amendment, I believe we need a secure border, and we need to deport illegal immigrants who break the law. ... The real difference between me and Sen. Graham is that I will stand up to my own party, and I will always put South Carolina first.”
Graham and Andrews are running for a full six-year Senate term; the winner will make history as the first female senator elected from South Carolina. The debate also featured Libertarian Kasie Whitener.

Graham shot back that she understands what people in her state are facing. When her parents died at a young age, Social Security benefits helped her and her brother survive. Graham said Andrews’ criticism of Trump’s “one big, beautiful bill” is misplaced because it lowered taxes on tips and Social Security. “You called it the one big, ugly bill, so here you are deceiving the people of South Carolina,” Graham said.
On affordability, Graham said she has “lived paycheck to paycheck” before and acknowledged that “gas prices are high right now. ... I feel the pain, too.” She said that she supports suspending the gas tax and that easing regulations on drilling would permanently bring prices down.

Andrews went right after Graham on the issue, nicknaming her “Data Center Darline.” Andrews said her data-center plan calls for a “two-year moratorium, protections to ensure your rates don’t go up and a return to real local control.”

“Under her Bernie Sanders plan, a two-year moratorium, that is dangerous to the national security of our country, because in two years China is going to be so far ahead [that] we are going to be in so much trouble,” Graham said, adding that local communities should decide whether data centers get built in their backyards.
“I want communities to decide. She wants the federal government to decide.”

items.title: What the Iran war has done to the world’s energy supply, in charts - Al Jazeera
items.summary: <a href="https://news.google.
items.content:
Share What the Iran war has done to the world’s energy supply, in charts on social media
A major energy conference is going ahead in Riyadh from Sunday despite a Houthi attack on the city’s King Khalid International Airport that killed 12 people and injured 309, according to Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation.
Saudi ⁠Arabia’s Ministry of Energy said on Sunday that the 25th ⁠World Petroleum Council Energy Congress has begun ‌in Riyadh. The 17th International Energy Forum (IEF) Ministerial will be held on the sidelines of the conference, called Riyadh Energy Week, which is to run until Thursday.
But Italy, the cohost of the IEF, will join the meeting via videolink. Nigeria, the other cohost, is sending a representative to the event.
The IEF brings together 68 countries that account for more than 90 percent of global oil and gas supplies and demand. Its members include Saudi Arabia, the United States and Russia. The meeting comes as the US-Israel war on Iran has disrupted energy flows and pushed governments to reassess their energy security.
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera looks at where the world’s energy comes from, how much is produced in the Middle East and which countries have strategic reserves to fall back on.
Energy heats our homes, fuels our cars, keeps the lights on and runs the factories that make what we buy. It comes from fossil fuels such as oil, coal and gas as well as nuclear power and renewables.
Despite rapid growth in renewables, fossil fuels still account for nearly 81 percent of global energy consumption. Oil is the largest source at 31.4 percent, followed by coal at 25.9 percent and natural gas at 23.5 percent. Traditional biomass, nuclear power and other sources make up the rest.
(Al Jazeera) Production is concentrated in a handful of regions, so disruptions in any of them ripple through global markets.
The Middle East is the largest oil-producing region, and North America is the largest natural gas producer. Russia and Central Asia are also major producers of both.
The Middle East’s importance to energy markets is also about geography. Three narrow waterways connect its producers with consumers around the world.
Before the Iran war, about 27 percent of global seaborne oil trade and almost 20 percent of liquefied natural gas trade transited through the Strait of Hormuz on the eastern side of the Arabian Peninsula.
On the peninsula’s western side, the Bab al-Mandeb strait links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, and the Suez Canal connects the Red Sea with the Mediterranean. As the Iran war has spilled over into other areas of the Middle East and Yemen’s civil war has ramped up, traffic has been reduced through both the strait and canal, forcing some energy shipments on longer routes around Africa.
(Al Jazeera) “That’s probably the first time we’ve really seen a major constriction of a chokepoint,” said Richard Matthews, director of consultancy and research at Gibson Shipbrokers, a London-based shipbroking and maritime advisory service.
He told Al Jazeera that what makes the Strait of Hormuz different from other chokepoints is “there is no alternative maritime route. There are some pipelines, but there’s no alternative, which is why it’s been so significant in terms of cargo volume.”
Gulf ports are where much of the region’s energy begins its journey to the rest of the world.
Further down the supply chain, people and businesses are feeling the disruption through the rising cost of essentials.
Countries that rely on oil, gas and fertiliser from the Gulf face higher prices, longer waits for shipments and the need to find other suppliers. Even where deals have kept goods moving, the extra costs are being passed down the chain.
Eritrea and Madagascar are the most dependent on Middle Eastern oil, each sourcing about 90 percent of their supply from the region. They are followed by Pakistan (78 percent), Japan (77 percent) and Kenya (77 percent).
Gas has been even harder to replace than oil because most of it travels as liquefied natural gas from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates through the Strait of Hormuz.
Countries that depend on these shipments are paying more for fuel and electricity and competing for a smaller pool of cargoes. Poorer importers with little storage have struggled the most to find alternatives.
The countries that rely most heavily on Middle Eastern gas are mostly in Asia. South Korea sources 31 percent of the gas it uses from the region, followed by India (29 percent), Pakistan (27 percent) and Taiwan (26 percent).
Countries keep emergency oil stocks for when supplies are cut off or reduced, and these have been the world’s main cushion during the war. That cushion is now wearing thin.
Western countries have little left to release, energy industry leaders warned, and the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve is at its lowest level since 1982.
“Estimates suggest less than 6 billion barrels of commercial inventories remain today with the vast majority not practically available,” Amin Nasser, head of Saudi Aramco, told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London on Monday.
The International Energy Agency, which coordinates emergency stocks for its members, released a record 400 million barrels of oil in March. It is now preparing to release another 100 million barrels of crude and diesel to ease soaring diesel prices although some of this may be oil from the March release that has yet to reach the market.
A storm in the Gulf of Mexico and attacks in Saudi Arabia are now threatening supplies again, keeping oil prices above $100 a barrel.
Before this year’s releases, China held by far the largest reserves, an estimated 1.4 billion barrels, more than the rest of the list combined. The US was second with 413 million barrels, followed by Japan with 263 million.

At the moment, the stock market is on the verge of doing something that no investor has witnessed in the last 156 years. Based on previous milestones leading to this point , trouble (and potentially a stock market crash) may be brewing.
Stock market valuations are approaching uncharted territory
Just as there's a laundry list of things going right for the stock market, there's also a long list of headwinds threatening to end Wall Street's AI-driven rally, such as rapidly rising margin debt , persistently elevated inflation, and surging long-duration bond yields.
But based solely on history, there's perhaps nothing more frightening for investors than premium stock valuations.
Defining "value" is tricky because there isn't a blueprint for evaluating every public company or the broader market. When individual investors evaluate and value businesses, they incorporate some degree of emotion and/or subjectivity. The absence of a one-size-fits-all value approach is what makes accurately predicting short-term directional moves in the Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite so challenging.
However, one time-tested valuation tool has done a remarkable job of providing investors with apples-to-apples comparisons of broad market valuations throughout history: the S&P 500's Shiller P/E Ratio, also known as the Cyclically Adjusted P/E Ratio ( CAPE Ratio ).
What gives the Shiller P/E Ratio a leg up over all other valuation tools is that it's based on average inflation-adjusted earnings over the last 10 years. Whereas earnings turning negative during recessions can make the traditional P/E ratio useless, this isn't the case with the Shiller P/E Ratio.
Stock Market Shiller PE Ratio on the verge of taking out its Dot Com Bubble all-time high 🚨 🤯 👀 https://t.co/CtCmSgWnLt
Though economists introduced this valuation tool in 1988, it's been backtested to January 1871, providing roughly 156 years of monthly valuation data. Over this time, the average Shiller P/E Ratio is a relatively modest 17.42. As of the closing bell on Oct. 5, the S&P 500's Shiller P/E clocked in at 41.67. That's within a stone's throw of its all-time high of 44.19, set in December 1999.
While making history is normally a good thing for the stock market, making valuation history is the exact opposite , according to historical precedent.
The first time the CAPE Ratio surpassed 30 was in August-September 1929. This two-month period of investing euphoria on Wall Street was followed by the Great Depression. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 89% of its value from peak to trough during the Great Depression.
Mind you, this isn't the only time the CAPE Ratio has surpassed 30 . The benchmark S&P 500 lost about 20% in the fourth quarter of 2018 after it topped 30, and the COVID-19 crash wiped away 34% of the S&P 500's value in just 33 calendar days in February-March 2020.
The first time the CAPE Ratio exceeded 40 was during the internet-driven hype. Mere months after peaking at 44.19, the dot-com bubble burst. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite had lost 49% and 78% of their respective values by October 2002.
Historical precedent isn't subtle. When stock valuations soar to never-before-seen premiums, generational downtrends and/or stock market crashes occur. The Shiller P/E Ratio is on the verge of making dubious history and crossing above 44.19 for the first time.
The good news: History works both ways and strongly favors optimists
Even though the Shiller P/E Ratio can't tell investors when the music will stop or what catalyst will pull the rug out from beneath a historically pricey stock market, the foreshadowing is crystal clear... over the short term. But when investors take a step back and examine the bigger picture, they'll find an entirely different story .
There's no question that stock market corrections, bear markets, and crashes can be scary and tug on investors' heartstrings. But these events share a common thread: they're relatively short-lived.
In late May, the analysts at Bespoke Investment Group examined the length of 27 separate S&P 500 bull and bear market events since the start of the Great Depression in September 1929. Bespoke's data set, published on X (formerly Twitter), highlights the night-and-day difference between optimism and pessimism on Wall Street.
In one corner, the average S&P 500 bear market reached its trough in 286 calendar days, or the equivalent of 9.5 months. Additionally, no bear market has lasted longer than 630 calendar days over the last 97 years.
The current bull market that began on 10/12/22 is now the 9th longest in S&P 500 history, surpassing the 1,324-day bull that ended on 2/9/1966: https://t.co/4mGsS2t2ft
By comparison, the typical S&P 500 bull market has persisted for an average of 1,023 calendar days, or approximately 3.6 times as long as the average bear market. What's more, 14 of 27 bull markets lasted longer than the aforementioned lengthiest bear market.
If nearly a century of research isn't enough, the analysts at Crestmont Research have you covered. They calculated the rolling 20-year total returns, including dividends, of the broad-based S&P 500 since 1900. Mind you, the S&P wasn't incepted until 1923, meaning researchers had to track the performance of its components in other major indexes from 1900 to 1923.
Crestmont's data set produced 107 rolling 20-year periods (1900-1919, 1901-1920, and so on, through 2006-2025). What's noteworthy is that all 107 generated a positive average annual total return .
Put another way, even if investors hypothetically purchased an S&P 500-tracking fund ahead of the Great Depression, the dot-com bubble, or other major downturns or crash events, their investment would have generated a positive total return every time if it had been held for 20 years .
Even if the stock market makes dubious valuation history, well over a century of total return data suggests that long-term, optimistic investors will be just fine.

Imran Khan’s party decries ‘coup’ after Pakistan suspends provincial government
Suspension of provincial government escalates standoff with Khan’s PTI party a week after his supporters began marching to demand his release
Pakistan has declared a state of emergency in a province ⁠led by Imran ​Khan’s PTI party and suspended its government, a move a party spokesperson described as “more of a coup disguised as emergency”.
President Asif Ali Zardari ​declared the emergency in the north-western Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Sunday, after the federal government said authorities there had failed to tackle Islamist militancy in the province bordering Afghanistan.
The state of emergency and imposition of a new governor in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa sharply escalates a standoff between ⁠Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party and the government, and comes a week after PTI supporters gathered in the province intending to march on Islamabad to demand Khan’s release.
Hundreds of activists and three of Khan’s sisters were detained before the planned march, in ​what the PTI called one of the strongest crackdowns in years.
Khan’s aide and PTI spokesperson Zulfikar Bukhari called the government’s move “more of a coup disguised as emergency,” adding that it risked inciting more bloodshed and instability and was intended to stop the protest.
Supporters of Imran Khan start march on locked-down Islamabad
Pakistan’s constitution ‌allows the government to take over from ‌provincial authorities during an emergency, and the law minister, Azam Nazeer Tarar, said a provincial governor would take charge in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which has suffered an increasing number ‌of militant attacks in recent months.
Tarar told a news conference in Islamabad that the governor will initially be in place for six months, but could stay for as long as needed. The interior ministry said it would be deploying troops in the province.
The federal government and the military accuse PTI of failing to curb militants. The party rejects the charge and says Islamabad has not provided the funding and equipment it needs.
Restrictions have been placed on the movements of Sohail Afridi, who had previously been in charge of the province, one of his close aides told Reuters.
Imran Khan’s sons accuse Pakistani army chief of vendetta against imprisoned father
Maulana Fazlur Rehman, leader of the JUI-F political party and engaged by the government to mediate with PTI, also condemned the move. “Imposition of emergency is an ambush on democracy,” he told a news conference in Islamabad.
In Islamabad, the government has deployed tens of thousands of security forces and lined roads with containers ready to block roads, to bar protesters from reaching parliament.
Candidates backed by Khan’s party won the most seats ⁠in the 2024 election but formed a government only in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Supporters of the 74-year-old former cricket star say ​the military rigged the vote against him, which the ​military denies.
Cases against Khan range from concerns over state ​gifts to instigating violence and an accusation of an unlawful marriage. All but one conviction have been suspended or overturned, ​with appeals pending. He denies wrongdoing.
President Zardari ​declared the emergency on the advice of ​the prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, after a cabinet decision, the president’s office said.
Sharif told the cabinet that security forces and citizens had been under attack for two years. “We can’t just act as a silent spectator.”
Islamabad also accuses Afghanistan of harboring militants who launch attacks inside Pakistan, and says PTI has sympathised with the Taliban in Kabul and its domestic affiliates. Both deny the charge.

items.title: Republican senator says Trump diesel agreement with Russia may be illegal
items.summary: US President Trump's bid to bring down diesel prices by easing sanctions on Russia prompts rare Republican criticism.
items.content:
Share Republican senator says Trump diesel agreement with Russia may be illegal on social media
A firefighter extinguishes the smoldering ruins of a house following a Russian guided aerial bomb attack that killed one person in Kharkiv, Ukraine, on October 11, 2026 [Sergey Bobok/AFP]
By Al Jazeera Staff , Reuters and The Associated Press
United States Senator Thom Tillis has questioned the legality of President Donald Trump’s decision to temporarily relax sanctions on Russian diesel , in an effort to bring down record-high fuel prices caused by the US-Israel war against Iran.
During a Sunday interview on the NBC News television show Meet the Press, Tillis argued that the sanctions relief could violate congressional law.
