“I do believe there’s a legitimate case for saying the president’s not following the law,” said Tillis.
Trump’s decision has unsettled some Republican lawmakers who continue to support Ukraine in its war with Russia, which began in February 2022, after Moscow launched a full-scale invasion of the eastern European country.
Tillis warned that his vote in support of Trump’s legislative priorities would be contingent on the White House reversing course.
“If the president wants my support, which I believe he should get for funding military operations and year-end funding beyond baseline funding, I think the president needs to understand this is a problem, and I’m not the only Republican concerned with this,” Tillis said.
Tillis has become a critical voice within the Republican Party, denouncing what he sees as overreach from the Trump administration.
But his time as a senator is nearly at a close. In June 2025, Tillis announced he would not be seeking re-election in the November 3 midterm elections, after Trump threatened him with a primary challenge in his home state of North Carolina. His term ends in January.
Separately on Sunday, Tillis joined a bipartisan group of senators in issuing a letter to denounce the sanctions relief for Russia.
The group included Republicans like Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and John Curtis of Utah, as well as Democrats Jeanne Shaheen and Richard Blumenthal.
“The United States should not provide [Russian President Vladimir] Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course,” the senators wrote.
Another retiring Republican lawmaker, Representative Don Bacon, also said on Friday that “propping up Putin’s war economy is morally wrong as he uses that money to bomb cities”.
The pushback points to schisms within the Republican Party over Russia’s invasion.
Figures from the party’s establishment wing have generally pressed for robust support for Kyiv , while other party members have been sceptical of continued US support for Ukraine.
Trump himself has been critical of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy , accusing the government in Kyiv of impeding a US-negotiated ceasefire.
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal, because he could have made many deals, and for some reason, he never does,” Trump said on Saturday. “That’s a war that should have never started, and I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
A day earlier, Trump had announced that a call with Putin had concluded with an agreement to provide 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the global marketplace, with a further 500,000 tonnes to be delivered in November.
In an interview with Fox and Friends on Sunday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent argued that the administration’s decision to ease some sanctions on Moscow was necessary to obtain relief from surging diesel prices .
“We’re going to do it with all the legal authorities we have,” Bessent said.
Analysts have said that the decision is unlikely to bring prices down in the long term. Critics like Tillis have also pointed to previous law barring the importation of Russian fuel, including a 2022 executive order.
A law signed last month — named after the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham — also prohibits US investment in the Russian energy sector.
This year’s rise in global fuel prices has largely been attributed to the US-Israel war against Iran, which began in February. As a result of that war, Iran has limited commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway for the fuel trade.
Tillis pointed to those circumstances in his remarks to Meet the Press.
“ If President Trump wants to end the strain on energy supplies, number one, get things right in Iran, and number two, recognise that it was Vladimir Putin, not Zelenskyy, that started this war,” Tillis said.
“It’s Vladimir Putin who owns the responsibility for energy prices to the extent that they come from that part of the world.”
Trump’s decision also garnered international criticism, with the office of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney issuing a statement in support of Ukraine.
“This agreement is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada, and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe,” Carney’s office said in a read-out of a call on Sunday with Zelenskyy. “It will provide additional revenue for Russia and help finance its illegal, unjustifiable war against Ukraine.”

Badawi Urges Sustained Oil and Gas Investment to Safeguard International Energy Supply | Egypt Oil & Gas
Badawi Urges Sustained Oil and Gas Investment to Safeguard International Energy Supply
Egypt’s Minister of Petroleum and Mineral Resources Karim Badawi urged continued investment in oil and natural gas exploration, production and infrastructure to bolster energy security during the 17th ministerial meeting of the International Energy Forum (IEF) in Riyadh, according to a statement by the Ministry of Petroleum and Mineral Resources (MoPMR).
Badawi stressed that energy security is a shared responsibility and cannot be achieved without sufficient investment in the oil and gas industries, calling for greater spending on exploration, production, infrastructure and technology.
Badawi outlined Egypt’s priorities for securing its energy needs, including increasing domestic oil and natural gas production by improving the investment climate and accelerating exploration, drilling and field development in cooperation with investment partners. He added that Egypt aimed to maximize the economic value of its petroleum resources by increasing refinery utilization and expanding petrochemical production and other value-added products.
The minister said natural gas remained a key component of Egypt’s energy mix, supporting electricity supply as the country integrated more renewable energy capacity, adding that Egypt is working to diversify supply sources, improve energy efficiency, rationalize consumption and expand renewable energy, while exploring emerging options such as hydrogen.
He sheds light on measures taken to improve the investment climate in the oil and natural gas sector, including settling outstanding payments to foreign partners, introducing new investment incentives, improving investment terms and making geological data and exploration opportunities more accessible through digital platforms such as the Egypt Upstream Gateway (EUG).
On the importance of regional cooperation and infrastructure connecting production sources with consumption centers and international market citing Cyprus’s Cronos gas field as an example of regional cooperation, noting that the project would enable Cypriot natural gas to be transported to Egypt for processing and liquefaction before being exported to European markets.
He added that the model could be extended to other Eastern Mediterranean resources, including Cyprus’s Aphrodite field and discoveries in Block 10.
The IEF’s 17th ministerial meeting was held in Riyadh, the Saudi Arabian capital, on October 11 under the theme “Energy Security and Shared Goals in a New Era.” The meeting was inaugurated by Saudi Minister of Energy Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman and IEF Secretary-General Jassim al-Shirawi.

items.content:
At the height of the recent crisis in the Middle East, the collapse of traffic through the Strait of Hormuz disrupted 14% of global oil and natural gas supply. Bypass pipelines, additional production and stock drawdowns covered more than half of the shortfall; lower consumption accounted for the rest. But not every country had the same room to maneuver. Those with ample reserves, alternative suppliers and the means to absorb higher costs could ride out the shock, while the rest competed for fewer, costlier cargo.
This disparity is central to “Aftershocks,” a study published on September 17 by the McKinsey Global Institute. It assesses 65 economies by their exposure to supply disruptions and their capacity to respond. The surge in freight rates pointed to the binding constraint: deliverability, not availability. A cargo of crude oil, refined products or LNG needs a suitable vessel, insurance and safe passage, and refining, storage or regasification capacity at its destination.
Greece already controls key links in this supply chain, possessing the world’s largest merchant fleet by carrying capacity, refineries and storage facilities, ports, and shipbuilding and repair yards. The EU’s Operation Aspides, whose area of operations has extended from the Red Sea to the Strait of Hormuz since 2024, is run from Larissa. Brussels’ maritime and ports strategies, adopted in March, treat such capabilities as integral to economic security, resilience and defense. What Greece still lacks is a permanent mechanism for coordination between the state and the shipping industry when supply chains break down.
Norway has relied on such a framework for decades. In 1940, its government assumed control of most of the merchant fleet outside German-controlled areas. The model was revived during the Cold War and took its present form in 2002 as Nortraship, a standing body linking government and shipowners, with an operational role in crises. When the war in Iran choked off energy flows, the security and preparedness department of the Norwegian Shipowners’ Association worked with the authorities and DNK, Norway’s war-risk insurer, to assess threats and keep companies informed. With that support, every Norwegian-linked vessel seeking to leave the Persian Gulf was out by the end of June.
A comparable Greek arrangement would provide real-time situational awareness of which Greek-owned vessels, by location, commitments and insurance cover, are available for charter in a supply emergency. It would speed their mobilization and the flow of security information, and track the status of ports, storage facilities, refineries and shipyards. Mobilization, however, depends on insurance: During the crisis, private underwriters canceled or sharply repriced war-risk cover, prompting Washington to announce a state-backed reinsurance facility. In May, an EU official stated that the bloc was considering state guarantees to help shipping companies with premiums, but no such EU initiative has yet been announced.
With Greek owners accounting for about three-fifths of the EU-controlled fleet, Athens has more at stake than any other member-state, and more standing to make the case for such an instrument in Brussels.

Last week, Araghchi said “there is no military solution” to the US war, adding, “only negotiations based on justice and fairness” could end the conflict.

Iranian and Saudi diplomatic ties have endured despite longstanding friction, with embassies restored under a 2023 Chinese-brokered agreement remaining operational. Before that breakthrough, a seven-year diplomatic rupture had fuelled regional proxy conflicts.

US President Donald Trump has been criticised for condemning Ukraine for its attacks on Russian refineries but not levelling the same criticism at Moscow for its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure [File: Eric Lee/Reuters]
United States President Donald Trump has called on Ukraine to replace Volodymyr Zelenskyy, lashing out at the Ukrainian leader for strikes on Russian oil refineries that have contributed to high global diesel prices.
The criticism on Saturday came as tensions between the US and Ukraine have risen after Trump announced a diesel supply deal with Russia.
list of 3 items list 1 of 3 Russia kills 20 in Ukraine as US hosts ‘productive’ talks to end war
list 2 of 3 Putin tells Trump peace talks are unlikely, cites Ukraine drone attacks
list 3 of 3 Why is US turning to Russia for diesel despite sanctions?
The steep rise in global fuel prices, which followed the outbreak of the US-Israel war on Iran, has become a political liability for Trump’s Republican Party as it heads into next month’s midterm elections, in which opposition Democrats could gain control of one or both houses of Congress.
“I think it’s ⁠time for Ukraine to get a new president,” Trump told reporters at the White House, saying Zelenskyy had hurt global diesel supplies with strikes on Russian refineries.
“He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers with diesel fuel because Russia supplies a large portion of the diesel fuel throughout the world,” Trump said.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, however, defended Zelenskyy in a post on X.
“He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide,” Sybiha wrote. “Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well. He deserves support.”
Trump, who has been urging Zelenskyy to stop attacking Russian energy infrastructure for weeks, struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday to buy diesel from Russia in an attempt to reduce high fuel prices.
The deal marked a stunning reversal of years of Washington’s pressure on Russia over its full scale invasion of Ukraine.
Trump has sought to blame record-high US diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the US-led war in Iran.
The US-Russia deal drew a furious reaction from Zelenskyy, who said it had emboldened Moscow. He linked the agreement with ⁠a Russian attack on Saturday that killed 20 people, including three children, in the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia.
“Today, Russia said thank you for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelenskyy said.
“Last night provided yet more confirmation that Russia perceives any easing of pressure as a signal that it can supposedly keep fighting, that it can supposedly keep dropping bombs on cities,” he said. “Different signals are needed.”
The Zaporizhzhia assault was the third mass-casualty attack on Ukraine in four days.
Nearly 80 ⁠civilians were killed in Russian strikes on Wednesday and Thursday, including at least 30 killed by a bomb in the eastern garrison city of ⁠Kramatorsk and 22 others by a missile in the town of Pryluky, about 130km (80 miles) east of Kyiv.
Trump’s announcement about the diesel deal was in stark contrast to a sweeping Russia sanctions law he signed last month aimed at clamping down on Moscow’s oil and gas revenues that fuel the war against Ukraine.
He announced the deal amid talks between Ukrainian and European officials with US negotiators in Miami, Florida, on Friday, which were aimed at developing ⁠a common proposal for ending the war, according to the Reuters news agency.
In his remarks at the White House, Trump criticised Zelenskyy over the lack of a peace deal while demanding an end to Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy facilities.
“I said to him, ‘Do what you want. Don’t hit refineries. There’s plenty of targets. Don’t ‌hit ‌refineries.’ And he went out and he hit,” Trump said. “He better damn well stop.”
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals, but for some reason, he never does,” Trump added.
The diesel deal was criticised by US lawmakers, including one of Trump’s fellow Republicans, Representative Don Bacon, who said it was time to apply more sanctions that Congress had recently passed, not roll them back.
Ukraine’s European allies have also expressed dismay at the Russian deal and said they stood by their commitment to sanctions.
United Kingdom Prime Minister Andy Burnham spoke with Zelenskyy on Saturday and said London would strengthen its sanctions on Russia, according to a Downing Street spokesperson.
Zelenskyy, meanwhile, said every additional $1bn Russia earns from exports would help pay for weapons components, drone upgrades, missile production and the recruitment of mercenaries and Moscow would only be ready to stop when its ability to fight diminished.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine was coordinating steps to counter the extra revenue Russia will receive and he had spoken to French President Emmanuel Macron about shoring up Ukraine’s air defences.
He went on to warn of an increased risk of further missile strikes in the coming days.
Zelenskyy also said he had discussed the developments with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Ukraine would receive ammunition in the coming days for the F-16 fighter jets used to intercept Russia’s Shahed drones.

items.title: Not Nvidia. Not Broadcom. This Little-Known Chip Supplier Could Be the AI Boom's Best-Kept Secret. - Yahoo Finance
items.summary: Not Nvidia. Not Broadcom. This Little-Known Chip Supplier Could Be the AI Boom's Best-Kept Secret.  Yahoo Finance
items.content:
Not Nvidia. Not Broadcom. This Little-Known Chip Supplier Could Be the AI Boom's Best-Kept Secret.
When investors think about the artificial intelligence boom, two names tend to dominate conversations. They are Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), which supplies the graphics processing units (GPUs) powering much of the AI industry, and Broadcom (NASDAQ: AVGO), which helps tech companies develop custom silicon. But there's a lesser-known player that could be the industry's best-kept secret: Cerebras Systems (NASDAQ: CBRS).
With Cerebras, it all starts with speed. Instead of the usual approach to chip design, Cerebras built its business around a large processor designed specifically for artificial intelligence : its Wafer-Scale Engine.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
Image source: Getty Images. The chip combines computing cores, memory, and communication capabilities into a single piece of silicon, reducing the need to move data between separate components. Through this approach, Cerebras aims to alleviate bottlenecks that can slow AI workloads.
That matters because training an AI model is only one part of the equation. Once a model is deployed, it's used for AI inference, answering questions, writing code, and even executing tasks for millions of users in real time. In fact, inference is becoming one of the fastest-growing trends in the AI market today.
Cerebras is investing in that shift by working to make AI responses faster.
As AI applications become more interactive, speed could become a huge competitive advantage. It could make conversations with AI chatbots faster and more fluid, while enabling AI agents to complete multi-step tasks more quickly, across domains ranging from software development and business workflows to scientific research.
The company's approach is already attracting attention from major AI players, including OpenAI.
Getting a major AI company to adopt its technology is a huge vote of confidence for any chipmaker. That's why Cerebras' relationship with OpenAI stands out.
The companies recently announced a multi-year agreement to deploy 750 megawatts of Cerebras compute capacity for OpenAI customers, with deployment planned in stages through 2028. The goal is to make AI responses faster, particularly for workloads that generate long answers, assist with coding, and power AI agents.
The partnership took an even bigger turn in August, when Cerebras announced that it's powering the Ultrafast mode for OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol. The company says the service can deliver up to 750 output tokens per second and run up to 14 times faster than with standard processing. This demonstrates how Cerebras' specialized hardware can greatly improve the user experience with advanced AI models.
For investors, the important point is that Cerebras' technology is already powering real commercial AI services, backed by one of the leading AI model providers. But proving its technology works is only part of the equation.
The company is also racing to build out its next-generation hardware.
Cerebras recently announced its CS-4 system, which it says can deliver up to twice the speed of its predecessor, along with improved efficiency and faster token generation. CS-4 is part of a broader platform that Cerebras says will allow it to upgrade computing, cooling, and power delivery more independently. That matters because performance doesn't depend on chips alone.
Data centers must also deliver enough power, move data efficiently, and cool dense hardware. As a result, by adopting this design, the company is trying to improve the economics of running AI at scale. That makes Cerebras' technology better suited for large deployments, especially as AI data centers become bigger and more complex.
For investors looking beyond the biggest chipmakers, this continued product development is another reason to watch the company.
Nvidia and Broadcom may be providing much of the infrastructure behind AI, but the AI boom is also creating opportunities for lesser-known chipmakers. That could mean room for more than one winning chip design.
Looking ahead, Cerebras' focus on speed and inference could give it a major role in the next phase of the AI boom, especially as it launches broader platforms that can scale with AI data centers.
If demand for faster AI keeps growing, Cerebras could turn out to be one of the market's strongest under-the-radar chip suppliers.

items.title: US justice department investigates TV networks over Trump pool coverage
items.summary: The White House had blocked access for CNN, MS Now and Politico, leading them to restrict pool coverage.
items.content:
Image caption, The row over the White House pool affected live TV coverage of Trump events last month
The US Department of Justice (DoJ) has said it is investigating several TV networks over whether they broke federal competition laws when they recently suspended pool coverage of Donald Trump.
Last month, five networks paused their presidential coverage for several days in response to the Trump administration withdrawing the credentials of reporters from CNN, MS Now and Politico.
The DoJ asked ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News to hand over communications related to the pool and said the boycott could violate the Sherman Act, referring to a law that bars companies from engaging in monopolistic business practices.
Pool members usually share their material with the wider media.
A DoJ spokesperson said: "The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these ânews organisations have violated the antitrust laws."
Trump blocked CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House last month after accusing the organisations of writing "fiction or lies" about his team.
The White House later reinstated their access following a judge's ruling. The three outlets had sued the Trump administration, arguing the restricted access violated their First Amendment rights.
The First Amendment forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press - language that courts have traditionally interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage.
The Trump administration has taken a number of legal actions against news publications in the US, including lawsuits over coverage of the president.
In February, the White House announced it was taking control of the press pool, which has access to Trump and had for more than a century been managed by the White House Correspondents' Association.
The same month, the Trump administration moved to bar Associated Press (AP) reporters and photographers from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because of the outlet's usage of the term "Gulf of Mexico" instead of "Gulf of America". AP filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing.

items.title: One killed, 11 injured in second Houthi strike on Riyadh airport in two days
items.summary: The Saudi capital has been hit by multiple attacks from the Iran-backed Yemeni group over the weekend.
items.content:
Figure caption, Watch: The scene at Riyadh international airport after strike
One person has been killed and 11 injured in a second strike on the international airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, officials have said.
A Saudi military spokesman said a projectile had hit King Khalid International Airport on Sunday, causing a fire in one of its passenger halls. Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said in a statement on X that one person, a Pakistani resident, had been killed in the attack.
It comes a day after a strike on the same airport killed 13 people and injured 308 others, following similar strikes earlier this week.
The Houthis in Yemen said they were behind the attacks and warned airlines and passengers against using Saudi Arabian airports and airspace.
The group said they had targeted the airport with a mix of ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as drones in the past 24 hours.
They also attacked oil facilities and Dammam airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, their military spokesman Brig Gen Yahya Saree said.
He vowed to continue the "escalating operations deep inside Saudi Arabia", warning that all Saudi airports were potential targets apart from those in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.
The Houthis have said they are targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war, as well as an air strike on the airport in Sanaa.
On Sunday Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition, said air defences had intercepted a missile near the airport in Riyadh, while authorities were dealing with the fire caused by an "unknown projectile" that hit Passenger Hall No 4.
US President Donald Trump has said the US would "make a decision" and "move very quickly" on whether to strike the Houthis, while UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting suggested the UK could "potentially" provide more support for Saudi Arabia.
Riyadh airport attack another dangerous moment in already tense conflict
Saturday's strike was the deadliest single attack on a Gulf Arab country since the war between Israel, the US and Iran began in February. The Saudi-led coalition vowed to respond, calling it a "war crime".
Four Saudi nationals, two people from Bangladesh and one person each from the US, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt were among the dead, the Saudi civil aviation authority said.
The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said on Sunday that an Indian man had succumbed to the injuries he sustained in the attack.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned the attacks and confirmed that a US citizen was killed in the strikes. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said he was "appalled".
The UK Foreign Office is advising against all travel to parts of Saudi Arabia, including areas within 10km (6.2 miles) of the border with Yemen, while other western embassies have warned their nationals about travel in the region.
Houthi-run Al Masirah TV said "the Saudi enemy" had launched an air strike on Sanaa International Airport in Yemen's capital. A residential home in the city was also struck, killing a child and injuring six people, the media outlet reported.
Saudi Arabia has not confirmed the attacks and the BBC has been unable to verify this report.
Abdullah Al-Alimi Bawazir, vice-president of Yemen's internationally recognised government, called for "decisive actions" from regional and international partners.
Riyadh's airport was struck on Thursday, an attack that killed three Saudi nationals . The Houthis claimed responsibility and said they had used cruise missiles to target the airport.
There were two other deadly attacks on Saudi airports in Abha and Riyadh in the two days prior to that.
Image caption, Smoke and flames seen at King Khalid airport in Riyadh on 8 October
The latest uptick in violence comes after a temporary ceasefire between the Houthis and Saudi-led forces, brokered in 2022, collapsed in July.
The conflict worsened after the Houthis seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive, prompting Saudi strikes. Yemeni pro-government forces later said they had secured the regions.
The Houthis currently control around a quarter of Yemeni territory and as much as 80% of the country's population. The Iran-backed armed group hopes to eventually seize complete control.
Saudi Arabia fears this would lead to the establishment of an Iranian satellite state on its southern border.
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told his Saudi Arabian counterpart on Sunday that his country was ready to provide assistance to "facilitate dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen", referring to the Houthi administration.

items.title: After oil increasingly left the Gulf, Iran is trying to regain its stranglehold on shipping - CNN
items.summary: After oil increasingly left the Gulf, Iran is trying to regain its stranglehold on shipping  CNN
items.content:
An aerial view shows ships anchored off the coast of Khasab in Oman's Musandam Governorate, near the Strait of Hormuz, on October 2.
Iran is stepping up attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and Persian Gulf in an effort to restore its leverage over the critical waterway.
There have been more than a dozen strikes on shipping since the end of September, reducing the volume of oil transiting the strait and keeping crude prices above $100 a barrel.
US President Donald Trump announced Thursday that he has no plans to strike Iran before the midterm elections, where rising energy costs could play a part in his Republican Party losing the House of Representatives, the Senate – or both.
“We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd,” Trump declared on Truth Social, adding that the administration is “having productive discussions” with Tehran and that his main goal is to ensure the country does not obtain a nuclear weapon.
Tehran, however, is focused on Hormuz as a “strategic red line” and is broadening its range of targets in the Gulf.
Leverage over Hormuz is non-negotiable for Tehran as it weathers US pressure despite a sinking economy. But Washington has said that the principle of free navigation in international waters is inviolable, a stance echoed by Gulf states that rely on the strait for much of their trade.
In one of the latest incidents, the National Guard of the United Arab Emirates said Saturday it had rescued 22 people following an oil tanker fire. Those rescued were Indian citizens – India is one of the largest suppliers of seafarers.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) – which tracks shipping incidents – has reported several other attacks in recent days.
It said the master of an outbound tanker reported it was struck Saturday by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, causing a fire on board. UKMTO reported another attack in the same area on Sunday, resulting in damage to the vessel. All crew members were reported safe.
An Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps serviceman salutes in front of an Iranian national flag.
The navy of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) claimed on Saturday that a supertanker carrying crude oil suffered a massive explosion after striking a naval mine while attempting to leave the Strait of Hormuz through a route Tehran hadn’t authorized.
“No extra-regional power has the right to threaten, maintain a domineering presence, or interfere in it. The Strait of Hormuz is Iran’s strategic red line,” said the head of the IRGC, Ahmed Vahidi, in a post on X.
UKMTO said Sunday it had also received a report from several ships in UAE waters that they had been directed via VHF radio messages to move from their anchorages. Iran has avoided targeting the UAE recently.
Shipping analysts Ambrey said the IRGC Navy had issued a warning to six vessels anchored around 16 miles (25 kilometers) from the port of Ras al Khaimah in the UAE.
“The vessels were advised to heave up anchor, exit the area immediately, and transit to Dubai anchorage,” Ambrey noted.
Analysts say the rise in Iranian attacks and threats is in response to higher volumes of oil and petroleum products through the strait. They averaged about 13.1 million barrels per day at the end of September, according to Kpler, a marine data tracking service.
That’s just under 80% of the 17.1 million barrels that had traveled through the strait each day before the war broke out.
But flows appear to have slowed this month. Just seven tankers transited the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, less than half the seven-day average and the lowest number since July 23, data from Kpler showed.
However, figures are at times revised higher after ships have moved through the strait, as many switch off their identification systems to try to avoid detection.
The US military continues to enforce a blockade on Iranian ports, as part of a strategy of maintaining economic pressure on Iran.
On Saturday it had disabled a cargo vessel in the Gulf of ⁠Oman after the ship’s crew ignored warnings and ⁠attempted to run the ongoing naval blockade against Iran.
“A U.S. military ‌fighter ⁠jet struck the stern of Panama-flagged M/V Ocean Molica (also known as the “Arika Sun”) with a precision ‌munition, fully disabling the ship’s propulsion without harming ⁠the crew,” US Central Command posted on X.
A man fuels a vehicle at a gas station in Alexandria, Virginia, on October 02, 2026. The U.S. national average for regular gasoline stood at about $4.40 per gallon on October 2, according to AAA, after September recorded its highest monthly average on record at $4.33 per gallon.
If the Strait of Hormuz is open, why are gas and diesel so expensive?
The US blockade has been highly effective, according to analysts. September was the first month that Iran loaded no crude onto tankers since maritime data tracking service Kpler began monitoring Iranian exports in 2013.
Last week, Mohsen Rezaei, Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, described the current economic situation as one of the most difficult periods the country has faced.
Tehran has insisted that if it can’t export its oil, its neighbors won’t be able to either. It believes it holds the initiative, given US shortages of air defense interceptors, and says its military posture has moved towards the offensive.
“Both the Americans and other countries should know: As we have said before, in a region where we cannot sell oil, no one else will be able to sell oil either. And if our security is not guaranteed, no infrastructure will be safe,” Iran’s chief negotiator Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf, said late in September.
It now seems intent on turning that threat into reality.

New Apple TV 4K, HomeView, and HomePod Mini: 16 Details Just Leaked
Sunday October 11, 2026 12:56 pm PDT by Joe Rossignol
Just two days before Apple's "Welcome home" experience in New York, Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman has leaked several details about the new products set to be unveiled, including an all-new smart home hub, a HomePod mini 2, and a new Apple TV 4K.
Here is an all-in-one summary of the details shared by Gurman:
Apple's home hub with a touch-enabled display will be named HomeView, seemingly confirming a trademark filing discovered by MacRumors .
HomeView is equipped with an A18 chip, which has 8GB of RAM in iPhones.
HomeView will be available in a tabletop version with a speaker base made of metal, as well as a wall-mounted version with a flat, square wall plate.
The tabletop HomeView will offer "better sound quality" than the HomePod mini.
The tabletop HomeView will be available in four finishes: Gray, Silver, Starlight, and Rose. The wall-mounted version will be limited to Gray and Silver.
HomeView will be unveiled this Tuesday, October 13, but the device is apparently not launching until "around mid-November."
HomeView will have a selection of Apple apps, but no App Store for third-party apps.
HomeView will be accompanied by an "Apple Home Collection" of accessories that brands such as LG and Schneider Electric developed in partnership with Apple. This will include a smart doorbell, deadbolt lock, thermostat, temperature sensor, indoor and outdoor security cameras, and a floodlight camera.
LG's accessories for the HomeView will not ship "until later this year at the earliest."
The new HomePod mini will be equipped with the Apple Watch Series 10's S10 chip, up from the S5 chip in the current model.
The new HomePod mini will be available in green, pink, blue, white, and midnight.
The new Apple TV 4K will be equipped with an A19 chip, which has 8GB of RAM.
The new Apple TV 4K may have built-in microphones for Siri AI.
The new Apple TV 4K may have an updated Siri Remote with a built-in speaker that makes it easier to find.
The new HomePod mini and Apple TV 4K models will be unveiled on October 13 and launch on Friday, October 30.
